editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div0.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of an audiotaped interview with William Frank Richardson, conducted by Ellen Richardson, on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview took place in Evansville, Indiana, and is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The interview was transcribed and processed by Greg Mizanin.

The reader should bear in mind that she or he is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of places, names, foreign words, and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: Transcribed and edited by Greg Mizanin July 9, 2003 I'm interviewing my grandfather William Frank Richardson in Evansville, Indiana at his home. And Ellen Richardson is me, the interviewer, and I'm going to start interviewing Frank Richardson.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: What branch did you serve in? In what war?

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: Okay. I served in World War II, and I was -- was drafted into the U.S. Navy. I was waiting to be called into the Naval Air Corps and they drafted me in the Navy, and because I was waiting to go into the Air Corps, they put me in the Navy instead of the Army. My first days of service were up at the Great Lakes Naval Academy in Great Lakes, Illinois, which is north of Chicago. We seemed to enjoy it. And the boot training was, as I remember it, twelve weeks, and we boarded a ship, too. I don't remember any of the instructors other than the fact we had to jump off a large height into water, which simulated jumping off the ship in case we had to. We -- I seemed to get along pretty good on that, and that was during the time of World War II, and at that time then we boarded a troop train and went to -- to California where we were loaded onto a personnel transport going to the Philippine Islands. We were originally going to another island, but they had a typhoon and which wrecked Okinowa and we went on to the Philippines at that time. There were no casualties in our unit. I got there the month the war was over -- over in Japan. We did see a Japanese that tried to slip into our chow line and they shot him and killed him, but that's the only casualty we saw. Some of the miserable -- memorable experiences were driving a landing craft, an LCVP, which is used for assault landing and so forth. And I was the captain of the -- captain of the ships, Gabe (ph), which was no more than just a landing craft vehicle personnel, and which they called an LCVP. While we were in the Philippines, it wasn't that bad. We had to go into the city to take our shower in the center of the city, and the natives would come up and try to borrow soap while we were showering, or they were wanting to trade cigarettes -- wanting to buy our cigarettes, which we had. As I remember, it was four cents a package at that time. The food wasn't bad, the Spam was all right, and we all got used to it and had to eat, but we always looked forward to having good food when we got back to state side. As far as the stress, I don't think we felt too much stress. We were young at that time. We had entertainers come over, Bob Hope and some of the others, and we'd sit on the side in an open amphitheater overlooking the Gulf of Leyte. We were on the island of Samar, which is part of the Philippines and about 30 miles away from the P.T. base -- boat base. We would travel -- During the service we couldn't get out of the area, but we did go to some fresh water rivers and swim because this was all salt water. We boarded several of the supply ships and just kind of took scavenger hunts through those, which we probably weren't allowed to, but we did. We picked up film and things of that nature. We'd go to the graveyards of the planes that were shot down and get some of the films out of that, and cut it up and use it in our cameras. They were all pushed into a pile in a salvage yard there. I do recall the day the service ended. That was a big, nice event. Everybody seemed to be happy. I was -- I was overseas at the time the service ended and got over there just as it was ending. And after I got out, I went back to Evansville College and schooled under -- under the G.I. Bill of Rights, went to Evansville College for one year taking engineering, and from there I transferred to Indiana University, where I joined the fraternity, the Lambda Chi Alpha (ph). We still have a lasting relationship with those members in the fraternity. In fact, we meet every summer at some place and there's at least 18 of us. We just completed our 52nd reunion. After getting out of school, I did join the Veterans, the VFW and the American Legion organizations, but I was not active in it. My later years, after I got out of college, I came back to Evansville, and first of all, I worked for a welding distributor, welding manufacturer in Aragat (ph), which is National Cylinder Gas, worked in Evansville, and then was transferred to St. Louis. The military influence -- experience did influence me in that I liked and enjoyed boats as I always done. I had no interest in joining the reserve unit although I was very close to being drafted again, but I was able to -- of course, I was overseas long enough that they didn't require me to join the reserve unit or go to an additional later war. I do not attend any of the reunions. In fact, I don't even hear from any of the people in the service that we were with, although I have pictures of them. I don't think the service affected my life at all or anything. I think we just about covered everything during my experience in the Navy at that point. I did enjoy it, and I think it was a great farming period in my life.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: When you were drafted, how old were you?

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: I believe I was 18 at that time when I was drafted. I was waiting to go into the Naval Air Corps, which I had enrolled in at the age of 17.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: Did the draft start at 17 or 18?

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: No, the draft started at 18. They had a local draft board here that just evaluated everyone and then called them up as they needed additional recruits.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: So, you said when the war ended you were overseas. Were you still in the Philippines or --

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: No, that's the only place I went to, the Philippines, instead of -- until the war was over, they put us -- they shipped us all over there immediately after training.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: What were you in the Philippines for? Like, any specific reason or were you just waiting to have to go over to Europe?

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: Well, we went to the Philippines to where we were needed, but we ended up in a ship repair base on the island of a -- Samar. It's part of Leyte, and it was a city called Manicany (ph). It was pretty, blue water -- green-blue water. It was very dirty. We got a lot of skin infections once we got in it. There was a lot of monsoon seasons, which was rainy seasons. It rained a lot. We cut holes in our shoes so that our feet would dry out -- and the top of our shoes.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: Did any of the Filipinos talk about, like, looking forward to like becoming a free country because the U.S. had just passed --

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: The Filipinos were kind of all natives and really didn't know how to speak English, so they couldn't communicate with us other than say, "Hey Joe," or something of this nature, you know. They were wanting -- always wanting to buy our soap that we had and we had barrels in the city streets we'd walk to get under to take a shower.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: Were you living in Evansville when you were drafted?

sp.speaker: William Frank Richardson
sp.p: Yes. I was living in Evansville when I was there. I graduated from Bausy (ph) High School at that time and was just going to Evansville College. [Tape recording turned off.] The boat that I drove was a landing craft vehicle, which carried a jeep and 50 men on it. It was two -- it had two -- two engines in it and two 20-millimeter guns on the stern, but it was -- it was a very stable boat, but the current was very strong at the time we'd come in to make our landings and so forth. I did enjoy it. It was very hot, and we didn't really wear shirts. We just -- just shorts only, basically. I did receive two -- developed two bad experiences while I was in the service because the drinking water wasn't very well. We all drank beer. We were issued beer chips and we'd go to the beer halls and have our beer. Also, we were able to get cigarettes very cheap and I learned to smoke at that time, too. So, those were the two bad habits for me -- problems that I did have in later life. In later life, not that I drank too much, but I did smoke a lot after I got out of the service, which now created a mild case of asthma.

sp.speaker: Ellen Richardson
sp.p: So that wraps up the interview.
